Distance-based (and path-based) covering problems for graphs of given cyclomatic number

The second and third authors were supported by the IDEX-ISITE initiative CAP 20-25 (ANR-16-IDEX-0001), the International Research Center “Innovation Transportation and Production Systems” of the I-SITE CAP 20-25, and the ANR project GRALMECO (ANR-21-CE48-0004). The third author was supported by the Jenny and Antti Wihuri Foundation, the Research Council of Finland grant number 338797.
Dibyayan Chakraborty Note: School of Computer Science, University of Leeds, United Kingdom.    Florent Foucaud Note: Université Clermont Auvergne, CNRS, Clermont Auvergne INP, Mines Saint-Étienne, LIMOS, 63000 Clermont-Ferrand, France.    Anni Hakanen 33footnotemark: 3 Note: Turku Collegium for Science, Medicine and Technology, University of Turku, Finland. Note: Department of Mathematics and Statistics, University of Turku, FI-20014, Finland.
Abstract

We study a large family of graph covering problems, whose definitions rely on distances, for graphs of bounded cyclomatic number (that is, the minimum number of edges that need to be removed from the graph to destroy all cycles). These problems include (but are not restricted to) three families of problems: (i) variants of metric dimension, where one wants to choose a small set SS of vertices of the graph such that every vertex is uniquely determined by its ordered vector of distances to the vertices of SS; (ii) variants of geodetic sets, where one wants to select a small set SS of vertices such that any vertex lies on some shortest path between two vertices of SS; (iii) variants of path covers, where one wants to select a small set of paths such that every vertex or edge belongs to one of the paths. We generalize and/or improve previous results in the area which show that the optimal values for these problems can be upper-bounded by a linear function of the cyclomatic number and the degree 1-vertices of the graph. To this end, we develop and enhance a technique recently introduced in [C. Lu, Q. Ye, C. Zhu. Algorithmic aspect on the minimum (weighted) doubly resolving set problem of graphs, Journal of Combinatorial Optimization 44:2029–2039, 2022] and give near-optimal bounds in several cases. This solves (in some cases fully, in some cases partially) some conjectures and open questions from the literature. The method, based on breadth-first search, is of algorithmic nature and thus, all the constructions can be computed in linear time. Our results also imply an algorithmic consequence for the computation of the optimal solutions: for some of the problems, they can be computed in polynomial time for graphs of bounded cyclomatic number.

1 Introduction

Distance-based covering problems in graphs are a central class of problems in graphs, both from a structural and from an algorithmic point of view, with numerous applications. Our aim is to study such problems for graphs of bounded cyclomatic number. The latter counts the number of edges that need to be removed from a graph to make it acyclic; it is a measure of sparsity of the graph that is popular in both structural and algorithmic graph theory [17, 47, 73] that has classic applications in program testing [57].

Although distance-based covering problems are very diverse, they share some properties that make them behave similarly in certain contexts, a fact that has already been observed for some of these problems, in particular, the metric dimension and the geodetic number problems [8, 29, 28]. Notably, regarding algorithmic applications, contrary to more “locally defined” problems, they often do not behave well for graphs of bounded treewidth [41, 44, 50]. The goal of this paper is to demonstrate that, for the more restrictive graphs of bounded cyclomatic number, interesting bounds can be derived, using a similar technique that is both simple and powerful. The obtained bounds also lead to efficient algorithms for these graphs. We will mainly focus on three types of such problems, as follows.

Metric dimension and its variants.

In these concepts, introduced in the 1970s [67, 36], the aim is to distinguish elements in a graph by using distances. A set S⊆V⁡(G)S\subseteq V(G) is a resolving set of GG if for all distinct vertices x,y∈V⁡(G)x,y\in V(G) there exists s∈Ss\in S such that d⁡(s,x)≠d⁡(s,y)d\left(s,x\right)\neq d\left(s,y\right). The smallest possible size of a resolving set of GG is called the metric dimension of GG (denoted by dim(G)\dim(G)). During the last two decades, many variants of resolving sets and metric dimension have been introduced. In addition to the original metric dimension, we consider the edge and mixed metric dimensions of graphs. A set S⊆V⁡(G)S\subseteq V(G) is an edge resolving set of GG if for all distinct edges x,y∈E⁡(G)x,y\in E(G) there exists s∈Ss\in S such that d⁡(s,x)≠d⁡(s,y)d\left(s,x\right)\neq d\left(s,y\right), where the distance from a vertex vv to an edge e=e1​e2e=e_{1}e_{2} is defined as min⁡{d⁡(v,e1),d⁡(v,e2)}\min\{d\left(v,e_{1}\right),d\left(v,e_{2}\right)\} [43]. A mixed resolving set is both a resolving set and an edge resolving set, but it must also distinguish vertices from edges and vice versa; a set S⊆V⁡(G)S\subseteq V(G) is a mixed resolving set of GG if for all distinct x,y∈V⁡(G)∪E⁡(G)x,y\in V(G)\cup E(G) there exists s∈Ss\in S such that d⁡(s,x)≠d⁡(s,y)d\left(s,x\right)\neq d\left(s,y\right) [42]. The edge metric dimension edim⁡(G)\mathrm{edim}(G) (resp. mixed metric dimension mdim⁡(G)\mathrm{mdim}(G)) is the smallest size of an edge resolving set (resp. mixed resolving set) of GG. More on the different variants of metric dimension and their applications (such as detection problems in networks, graph isomorphism, coin-weighing problems or machine learning) can be found in the recent surveys [48, 70].

Geodetic numbers.

A geodetic set of a graph GG is a set SS of vertices such that any vertex of GG lies on some shortest path between two vertices of SS [35]. The geodetic number g⁡(G)g\left(G\right) of GG is the smallest possible size of a geodetic set of GG.

The version where the edges must be covered is called an edge-geodetic set [4]. “Strong” versions of these notions have been studied. A strong (edge-) geodetic set of graph GG is a set SS of vertices of GG such that we can assign for any pair x,yx,y of vertices of SS a shortest x​yxy-path such that each vertex (edge) of GG lies on one of the chosen paths [3, 51, 54].

Recently, the concept of monitoring edge-geodetic set was introduced in [33] (see also [9, 20, 32, 37]) as a strengthening of a strong edge-geodetic set: here, for every edge ee, there must exist two vertices x,yx,y in the monitoring edge-geodetic set such that ee lies on all shortest paths between xx and yy.

These concepts have numerous applications related to the field of convexity in graphs, see the book [60].

We also consider the concept of distance-edge-monitoring-sets introduced in [30, 31] and further studied in [38, 74, 75], which can be seen as a relaxation of monitoring edge-geodetic sets. A set SS is a distance-edge-monitoring-set if, for every edge ee of GG, there is a vertex xx of SS and a vertex yy of GG such that ee lies on all shortest paths between xx and yy.

Path covering and partition problems.

In this type of problem, one wishes to cover the vertices (or edges) of a graph using a small number of paths. For path partition problems, the paths are required to be vertex-disjoint, but for path covering, they may not be. A path cover (path partition, respectively) is a set of (vertex-disjoint) paths of a graph GG such that every vertex of GG belongs to one of the paths. If one path suffices, the graph is said to be Hamiltonian, and deciding this property is one of the most fundamental graph-algorithmic problems. The paths may be required to be shortest paths, in which case we have the notion of an isometric path cover/partition [12, 13, 21, 25, 27, 69]; if they are required to be chordless, we have an induced path cover/partition [25, 49, 55]. The edge-covering versions have also been studied [2]. This type of problems has numerous applications, such as program and circuit testing [2, 58], vehicle routing [72] or bioinformatics [11]. They are the subject of well-known studies in graph theory, such as the Gallai-Milgram theorem [34] or conjectures by Berge [7] and Gallai [52].

Our goal.

Our objective is to study the three above classes of problems, on graphs of bounded cyclomatic number. (See Figure 1 for a diagram showing the relationships between the optimal solution sizes of the studied problems.) A feedback edge set of a graph GG is a set of edges whose removal turns GG into a forest. The smallest size of such a set, denoted by c⁡(G)c\left(G\right), is the cyclomatic number of GG [6]. It is sometimes called the feedback edge (set) number or the cycle rank of GG. For a graph GG on nn vertices, mm edges and kk connected components, it is not difficult to see that we have c⁡(G)=m−n+kc\left(G\right)=m-n+k, since a forest on nn vertices with kk components has n−kn-k edges. In this paper, we assume all our graphs to be connected. To find an optimal feedback edge set of a connected graph, it suffices to consider a spanning tree; the edges not belonging to the spanning tree form a minimum-size feedback edge set.

Graphs whose cyclomatic number is constant have a relatively simple structure. They are sparse (in the sense that they have a linear number of edges). They also have bounded treewidth (indeed the treewidth is at most the cyclomatic number plus one), a parameter that plays a central role in the area of graph algorithms, see for example Courcelle’s celebrated theorem [18]. Thus, they are studied extensively from the perspective of algorithms (for example for the metric dimension [24], the geodetic number [44] or other graph problems [17, 19, 26, 47, 71]). In particular, in many cases, distance-related problems are computationally hard on graphs of bounded treewidth [40, 41, 44, 50]. Thus, for this type of problems, it is of interest to design efficient algorithms for graphs of bounded cyclomatic number. Graphs of given cyclomatic number are also studied from a more structural angle [1, 64, 65, 66, 73].

Conjectures addressed in this paper.

In order to formally present the conjectures, we need to introduce some structural concepts and notations. A leaf of a graph GG is a vertex of degree 1, and the number of leaves of GG is denoted by ℓ⁡(G)\ell\left(G\right). Consider a vertex v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G) of degree at least 3. A leg attached to the vertex vv is a path p1​…​pkp_{1}\ldots p_{k} such that p1p_{1} is adjacent to vv, deg⁡(pk)=1\deg(p_{k})=1 and deg⁡(pi)=2\deg(p_{i})=2 for all i≠ki\neq k. The number of legs attached to the vertex vv is denoted by l⁡(v)l\left(v\right).

A set R⊆V⁡(G)R\subseteq V(G) is a branch-resolving set of GG, if for every vertex v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G) of degree at least 3 the set RR contains at least one element from at least l⁡(v)−1l\left(v\right)-1 legs attached to vv. The minimum cardinality of a branch-resolving set of GG is denoted by L⁡(G)L\left(G\right), and we have

L⁡(G)=∑v∈V⁡(G),deg⁡(v)≥3,l⁡(v)>1(l⁡(v)−1).L\left(G\right)=\sum_{v\in V(G),\,\deg(v)\geq 3,\,l\left(v\right)>1}(l\left(v\right)-1).

It is well-known that for any tree TT with at least one vertex of degree 3, we have dim(T)=L⁡(T)\dim(T)=L\left(T\right) (and if TT is a path, then dim(T)=1\dim(T)=1) [15, 36, 45, 67]. This has motivated the following conjecture.

Conjecture 1 ([66]).

Let GG be a connected graph with c⁡(G)≥2c\left(G\right)\geq 2. Then dim(G)≤L⁡(G)+2​c​(G)\dim(G)\leq L\left(G\right)+2c\left(G\right) and edim⁡(G)≤L⁡(G)+2​c​(G)\mathrm{edim}(G)\leq L\left(G\right)+2c\left(G\right).

The restriction c⁡(G)≥2c\left(G\right)\geq 2 is missing from the original formulation of Conjecture 1 in [66]. However, Sedlar and Škrekovski have communicated to us that this restriction should be included in the conjecture. Conjecture 1 holds for cacti with c⁡(G)≥2c\left(G\right)\geq 2 [66]. The bound dim(G)≤L⁡(G)+18​c​(G)−18\dim(G)\leq L\left(G\right)+18c\left(G\right)-18 was shown in [24] (for c⁡(G)≥2c\left(G\right)\geq 2), and is the first bound established for the metric dimension in terms of L⁡(G)L\left(G\right) and c⁡(G)c\left(G\right) (note that the bound holds even for a vertex-weighted variant of metric dimension). The bound dim(G)≤L⁡(G)+6​c​(G)\dim(G)\leq L\left(G\right)+6c(G) was proved in [10].

Sedlar and Škrekovski [65] also posed the following refinement of the previous conjecture, where δ⁡(G)\delta(G) is the minimum degree of GG.

Conjecture 2 ([65]).

If δ⁡(G)≥2\delta(G)\geq 2 and G≠CnG\neq C_{n}, then dim(G)≤2​c​(G)−1\dim(G)\leq 2c\left(G\right)-1 and edim⁡(G)≤2​c​(G)−1\mathrm{edim}(G)\leq 2c\left(G\right)-1.

In [65], Sedlar and Škrekovski showed that Conjecture 2 holds for graphs with minimum degree at least 3. They also showed that if Conjecture 2 holds for all 2-connected graphs, then it holds for all graphs GG with δ⁡(G)≥2\delta(G)\geq 2. Recently, Lu at al. [53] addressed Conjecture 2 and showed that dim(G)≤2​c​(G)+1\dim(G)\leq 2c(G)+1 when GG has minimum degree at least 2.

Conjecture 3 ([64]).

Let GG be a connected graph. If G≠CnG\neq C_{n}, then mdim⁡(G)≤ℓ⁡(G)+2​c​(G)\mathrm{mdim}(G)\leq\ell\left(G\right)+2c\left(G\right).

Conjecture 3 is known to hold for trees [42], cacti and 3-connected graphs [64], and balanced theta graphs [63].

The following conjecture on distance-edge-monitoring sets was also posed recently.

Conjecture 4 ([30, 31]).

For any graph GG, dem⁡(G)≤c⁡(G)+1\mathrm{dem}\left(G\right)\leq c\left(G\right)+1.

Here, dem⁡(G)\mathrm{dem}\left(G\right) is the the smallest size of a distance-edge-monitoring set of graph GG. The original authors of the conjecture proved the bound when c⁡(G)≤2c\left(G\right)\leq 2, and proved that the bound dem⁡(G)≤2​c​(G)−2\mathrm{dem}\left(G\right)\leq 2c\left(G\right)-2 holds when c⁡(G)≥3c\left(G\right)\geq 3 [30]. The conjectured bound would be tight [30, 31].

Regarding monitoring edge-geodetic sets, although no formal conjecture was explicitly posed, the bound meg⁡(G)≤9​c​(G)+ℓ⁡(G)−8\mathrm{meg}\left(G\right)\leq 9c\left(G\right)+\ell\left(G\right)-8 was proved in [20, 33], and it was asked whether this can be improved.

Our contributions.

In this paper, we are motivated by Conjectures 1-4, which we address. We will show that both dim(G)\dim(G) and edim⁡(G)\mathrm{edim}(G) are bounded from above by L⁡(G)+2​c​(G)+1L\left(G\right)+2c\left(G\right)+1 for all connected graphs GG. Moreover, we show that if L⁡(G)≠0L\left(G\right)\neq 0, then the bounds of Conjecture 1 hold.

We show that Conjecture 3 is true when δ⁡(G)=1\delta(G)=1, and when δ⁡(G)≥2\delta(G)\geq 2 and GG contains a cut-vertex. We also show that mdim⁡(G)≤2​c​(G)+1\mathrm{mdim}(G)\leq 2c\left(G\right)+1 in all other cases. We also consider the first part of Conjecture 1, that dim(G)≤L⁡(G)+2​c​(G)\dim(G)\leq L\left(G\right)+2c\left(G\right) from [66], in the case where δ⁡(G)=1\delta(G)=1, and we show that it is true when L⁡(G)≥1L\left(G\right)\geq 1 and otherwise we have dim(G)≤2​c​(G)+1\dim(G)\leq 2c\left(G\right)+1. We also consider the conjecture that edim⁡(G)≤L⁡(G)+2​c​(G)\mathrm{edim}(G)\leq L\left(G\right)+2c\left(G\right) from [66], and we show that it is true when δ⁡(G)=1\delta(G)=1 and L⁡(G)≥1L\left(G\right)\geq 1, and when δ⁡(G)≥2\delta(G)\geq 2 and GG contains a cut-vertex. We also show that edim⁡(G)≤2​c​(G)+1\mathrm{edim}(G)\leq 2c\left(G\right)+1 in all other cases.

Thus, our results yield significant improvements towards the Conjectures 1-3, since they are shown to be true in most cases, and are approximated by an additive term of 1 for all graphs.

Moreover, we also resolve in the affirmative Conjecture 4.

To obtain the above results, we develop a technique from [53], who introduced it in order to study a strengthening of metric dimension called doubly resolving sets in the context of graphs of minimum degree 2. We notice that the technique can be adapted to work for all graphs and in fact it applies to many types of problems: (variants of) metric dimension, (variants of) geodetic sets, and path-covering problems. For all these problems, the technique yields upper bounds of the form a⋅c⁡(G)+f⁡(ℓ⁡(G))a\cdot c\left(G\right)+f(\ell(G)), where ℓ⁡(G)\ell(G) is the number of leaves of GG, ff is a linear function that depends on the respective problem, and aa is a small constant.

The technique is based on a breadth-first-search rooted at a specific vertex, that enables to compute an optimal feedback edge set FF by considering the edges of the graph that are not part of the breadth-first-search spanning tree. We then select vertices of the edges of FF (or neighbouring vertices); the way to select these vertices depends on the problem. For the metric dimension and path-covering problems, a pre-processing is done to handle the leaves of the graph (for the geodetic set variants, all leaves must be part of the solution). Our results demonstrate that the techniques used by most previous works to handle graphs of bounded cyclomatic number were not precise enough, and the simple technique we employ is much more effective. We believe that it can be used with sucess in similar contexts in the future.

A preliminary version of this paper (without most of the proofs) appeared in the proceedings of the FCT 2023 conference [14].

Algorithmic applications.

For all the considered problems, our method in fact implies that the optimal solutions can be computed in polynomial time for graphs with bounded cyclomatic number. In other words, we obtain XP algorithms with respect to the cyclomatic number. This was already observed in [24] for the metric dimension (thanks to our improved bounds, we now obtain a better running time, however it should be noted that in [24] the more general weighted version of the problem was considered).

Organisation.

We first describe the general method to compute the special feedback edge set in Section 2. We then use it in Section 3 for the metric dimension and its variants. We then turn to geodetic sets and its variants in Section 4, and to path-covering problems in Section 5. We describe the algorithmic consequence in Section 6, and conclude in Section 7.

2 The general method

The length of a path PP, denoted by |P||P|, is the number of its vertices minus one. A path is induced if there are no graph edges joining non-consecutive vertices. A path is isometric if it is a shortest path between its endpoints. For two vertices u,vu,v of a graph GG, d⁡(u,v)d\left(u,v\right) denotes the length of an isometric path between uu and vv. Let rr be a vertex of GG. An edge e=u​v∈E⁡(G)e=uv\in E(G) is a horizontal edge with respect to rr if d⁡(u,r)=d⁡(v,r)d\left(u,r\right)=d\left(v,r\right) (otherwise, it is a vertical edge). For a vertex uu of GG, let Br​(u)B_{r}(u) denote the set of edges u​v∈E⁡(G)uv\in E(G) such that d⁡(u,r)=d⁡(v,r)+1d\left(u,r\right)=d\left(v,r\right)+1, i.e., the vertical edges where one endpoint is uu and the other endpoint vv is closer to rr than uu. A set FF of edges of GG is good with respect to rr if FF contains all horizontal edges with respect to rr and for each u≠ru\neq r, |Br​(u)∩F|=|Br​(u)|−1|B_{r}(u)\cap F|=|B_{r}(u)|-1. A set FF of edges is simply good if FF is good with respect to some vertex r∈V⁡(G)r\in V(G). For a set FF of good edges of a graph GG, let TFT_{F} denote the subgraph of GG obtained by removing the edges of FF from GG.

For example, consider the graph in Figure 2. We have rooted the graph at vertex rr, and the vertices at the same distance from rr are on the same level next to each other. Drawn this way, the horizontal edges with respect to rr are horizontal and the vertical edges are either vertical or diagonal. For example, the edge v1​v2v_{1}v_{2} is a horizontal edge since the distance from rr is 33 to both of its endpoints. The vertex v3v_{3} is an endpoint to three vertical edges but no horizontal edges. The set Br​(u)B_{r}(u) consists of vertical edges whose endpoint is uu and the other endpoint is a vertex on the level above uu. For example, Br​(v3)B_{r}(v_{3}) consists of the two vertical edges between v3v_{3} and two of the neighbors of rr. The third vertical edge incident with v3v_{3}, v1​v3v_{1}v_{3}, is not included in this set since v1v_{1} is further away from rr and, in fact, we have v1​v3∈Br​(v1)v_{1}v_{3}\in B_{r}(v_{1}). Notice that the sets Br​(u)B_{r}(u) form a partition of the vertical edges. The red edges form a good edge set with respect to rr as it contains all horizontal edges and the required number of vertical edges.

Lemma 5.

For any connected graph GG with nn vertices and mm edges and a vertex r∈V⁡(G)r\in V(G), a set FF of good edges with respect to rr can be computed in O⁡(n+m)O(n+m) time.

Proof.

By doing a Breadth First Search on GG from rr, distances of rr from uu for all u∈V⁡(G)u\in V(G) can be computed in O⁡(n+m)O(n+m) time. Then the horizontal and vertical edges can be computed in O⁡(m)O(m) time. Then the sets Br​(u)B_{r}(u) for all u∈V⁡(G)u\in V(G) can be computed in O⁡(n+m)O(n+m) time. Hence the set of good edges with respect to rr can be computed in O⁡(n+m)O(n+m) time. ∎

Lemma 6.

For a set FF of good edges with respect to a vertex rr of a connected graph GG, the subgraph TFT_{F} is a tree rooted at rr. Moreover, every path from rr to a leaf of TFT_{F} is an isometric path in GG.

Proof.

First observe that TFT_{F} is connected, as each vertex uu has exactly one edge u​v∈E⁡(TF)uv\in E(T_{F}) with d⁡(u,r)=d⁡(v,r)+1d\left(u,r\right)=d\left(v,r\right)+1. Indeed, removing horizontal edges or edges in Br​(u)B_{r}(u) does not affect the sets Br​(u′)B_{r}(u^{\prime}) where u′≠uu^{\prime}\neq u. Now assume for contradiction that TFT_{F} has a cycle CC. Let v∈V⁡(C)v\in V(C) be a vertex that is furthest from rr among all vertices of CC. Formally, vv is a vertex such that d⁡(r,v)=max⁡{d⁡(r,w):w∈V⁡(C)}d\left(r,v\right)=\max\{d\left(r,w\right)\colon w\in V(C)\}. Let E′E^{\prime} denote the set of edges in TFT_{F} incident with vv. Observe that |E′||E^{\prime}| is at least two. Hence either E′E^{\prime} contains an horizontal edge, or E′∩Br​(v)E^{\prime}\cap B_{r}(v) contains at least two edges. Either case contradicts that FF is a good edge set with respect to rr. This proves the first part of the observation.

Now consider a path PP from rr to a leaf vv of TFT_{F} and write it as u1​u2​…​uku_{1}u_{2}\ldots u_{k} where u1=ru_{1}=r and uk=vu_{k}=v. By definition, we have d⁡(r,ui)=d⁡(r,ui−1)+1d\left(r,u_{i}\right)=d\left(r,u_{i-1}\right)+1 for each i∈[2,k]i\in[2,k]. Hence, PP is an isometric path in GG. ∎

Observation 7.

Any set FF of good edges of a connected graph GG is a feedback edge set of GG with minimum cardinality.

Proof.

Due to Lemma 6 we have that TFT_{F} is a tree and therefore |F|=m−n+1|F|=m-n+1 which is same as the cardinality of a feedback edge set of GG with minimum cardinality. ∎

The base graph [24] GbG_{b} of a graph GG is the graph obtained from GG by iteratively removing vertices of degree 11 until there remain no such vertices. We use the base graph in some cases where preprocessing the leaves and other tree-like structures is needed.

3 Metric dimension and variants

In this section, we consider three metric dimension variants and conjectures regarding them and the cyclomatic number. We shall use the following result.

Distinct vertices x,yx,y are doubly resolved by v,u∈V⁡(G)v,u\in V(G) if d⁡(v,x)−d⁡(v,y)≠d⁡(u,x)−d⁡(u,y)d\left(v,x\right)-d\left(v,y\right)\neq d\left(u,x\right)-d\left(u,y\right). A set S⊆V⁡(G)S\subseteq V(G) is a doubly resolving set of GG if every pair of distinct vertices of GG are doubly resolved by a pair of vertices in SS. Lu et al. [53] constructed a doubly resolving set of GG with δ⁡(G)≥2\delta(G)\geq 2 by finding a good edge set with respect to a root r∈V⁡(G)r\in V(G) using breadth-first search. We state a result obtained by Lu et al. [53] using the terminologies of this paper.

Theorem 8 ([53]).

Let GG be a connected graph such that δ⁡(G)≥2\delta(G)\geq 2 and r∈V⁡(G)r\in V(G). Let S⊆V⁡(G)S\subseteq V(G) consist of rr and the endpoints of the edges of a good edge set with respect to rr.

  1. (i)

    The set SS is a doubly resolving set of GG.

  2. (ii)

    If rr is a cut-vertex, then the set S∖{r}S\setminus\{r\} is a doubly resolving set of GG.

  3. (iii)

    We have |S|≤2​c​(G)+1|S|\leq 2c\left(G\right)+1.

A doubly resolving set of GG is also a resolving set of GG, and thus dim(G)≤2​c​(G)+1\dim(G)\leq 2c\left(G\right)+1 when δ⁡(G)≥2\delta(G)\geq 2 due to Theorem 8. Moreover, if GG contains a cut-vertex and δ⁡(G)≥2\delta(G)\geq 2, we have dim(G)≤2​c​(G)\dim(G)\leq 2c\left(G\right). Notice that δ⁡(G)≥2\delta(G)\geq 2 implies that L⁡(G)=0L(G)=0. Therefore, Theorem 8 implies that Conjecture 1 holds for the metric dimension of a graph with δ⁡(G)≥2\delta(G)\geq 2 and at least one cut-vertex. When δ⁡(G)≥2\delta(G)\geq 2 and the graph has no cut-vertex, we are +1+1 away from the bound in Conjecture 1.

A doubly resolving set is not necessarily an edge resolving set or a mixed resolving set. Thus, more work is required to show that edge and mixed resolving sets can be constructed with good edge sets. A layer of GG is a set Ld={v∈V⁡(G)|d⁡(r,v)=d}L_{d}=\{v\in V(G)\ |\ d\left(r,v\right)=d\} where rr is the chosen root and dd is a fixed distance.

Proposition 9.

Let GG be a graph with δ⁡(G)≥2\delta(G)\geq 2, and let r∈V⁡(G)r\in V(G). If the set SS contains rr and the endpoints of a good edge set FF with respect to rr, then SS is an edge resolving set.

Proof.

Suppose to the contrary that there exist distinct edges e=e1​e2e=e_{1}e_{2} and f=f1​f2f=f_{1}f_{2} that are not resolved by SS. In particular, we have d⁡(r,e)=d⁡(r,f)d\left(r,e\right)=d\left(r,f\right). Due to this, say, e1e_{1} and f1f_{1} are in the same layer LdL_{d}, and e2e_{2} and f2f_{2} are in Ld∪Ld+1L_{d}\cup L_{d+1}. If ee is a horizontal edge with respect to rr, then e1,e2∈Se_{1},e_{2}\in S and ee and ff are resolved. Thus, neither ee nor ff is a horizontal edge with respect to rr and we have e2,f2∈Ld+1e_{2},f_{2}\in L_{d+1}.

If e2=f2e_{2}=f_{2}, then e,f∈Br​(e2)e,f\in B_{r}(e_{2}). Thus, we have e2∈Se_{2}\in S and at least one of e1e_{1} and f1f_{1} is also in SS. Now ee and ff are resolved by e1e_{1} or f1f_{1}. Therefore, we have e2≠f2e_{2}\neq f_{2} and e2,f2∉Se_{2},f_{2}\notin S.

Let w∈V⁡(G)w\in V(G) be a leaf in TFT_{F} such that e2e_{2} lies on a path between ww and rr in TFT_{F}. Since δ⁡(G)≥2\delta(G)\geq 2, the vertex ww is an endpoint of some edge in FF, and thus w∈Sw\in S. Since ee and ff are not resolved by SS, we have d⁡(w,f2)=d⁡(w,e2)=d′−d−1d\left(w,f_{2}\right)=d\left(w,e_{2}\right)=d^{\prime}-d-1, where w∈Ld′w\in L_{d^{\prime}}, due to the path between ww and rr being isometric (Lemma 6). Let PfP_{f} be an isometric path w−f2w-f_{2} in GG, and assume that PfP_{f} is such that it contains an element of SS as close to f2f_{2} as possible. Denote this element of SS by ss. We have s∈Lis\in L_{i} for some d+1<i≤d′d+1<i\leq d^{\prime} (notice that we may have s=ws=w). As the edges ee and ff are not resolved by SS, we have d⁡(s,e)=d⁡(s,f)d\left(s,e\right)=d\left(s,f\right), which implies that d⁡(s,e2)=d⁡(s,f2)=i−d−1d\left(s,e_{2}\right)=d\left(s,f_{2}\right)=i-d-1. Let Pe′P_{e}^{\prime} and Pf′P_{f}^{\prime} be isometric paths s−e2s-e_{2} and s−f2s-f_{2}, respectively. The paths Pe′P_{e}^{\prime} and Pf′P_{f}^{\prime} are internally vertex disjoint, since otherwise the vertex after which the paths diverge is an element of SS which contradicts the choice of PfP_{f} and ss. Let vev_{e} and vfv_{f} be the vertices adjacent to ss in Pe′P_{e}^{\prime} and Pf′P_{f}^{\prime}, respectively. Now, we have s​ve,s​vf∈Br​(s)sv_{e},sv_{f}\in B_{r}(s), and thus ve∈Sv_{e}\in S (otherwise, vf∈Sv_{f}\in S, which contradicts the choice of PfP_{f} and ss). If d⁡(ve,e2)<d⁡(ve,f2)d\left(v_{e},e_{2}\right)<d\left(v_{e},f_{2}\right), then vev_{e} resolves ee and ff, a contradiction. Thus, we have d⁡(ve,e2)≥d⁡(ve,f2)d\left(v_{e},e_{2}\right)\geq d\left(v_{e},f_{2}\right), but now there exists an isometric path w−f2w-f_{2} that contains vev_{e}, which is closer to f2f_{2} than ss is, a contradiction. ∎

Proposition 10.

Let GG be a graph with δ⁡(G)≥2\delta(G)\geq 2, and let r∈V⁡(G)r\in V(G). If the set SS contains rr and the endpoints of a good edge set FF with respect to rr, then SS is a mixed resolving set.

Proof.

The set SS resolves all pairs of distinct vertices by Theorem 8 and all pairs of distinct edges by Proposition 9. Therefore we only need to show that all pairs consisting of a vertex and an edge are resolved.

Suppose to the contrary that v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G) and e=e1​e2∈E⁡(G)e=e_{1}e_{2}\in E(G) are not resolved by SS. In particular, the root rr does not resolve vv and ee, and thus v,e1∈Ldv,e_{1}\in L_{d} for some d≥1d\geq 1. If ee is a horizontal edge, then e1,e2∈Se_{1},e_{2}\in S and ee and vv are resolved. Thus, assume that e2∈Ld+1e_{2}\in L_{d+1}. Let w∈V⁡(G)w\in V(G) be a leaf in TFT_{F} such that e2e_{2} lies on a path between ww and rr in TFT_{F}. Since δ⁡(G)≥2\delta(G)\geq 2, the vertex ww is an endpoint of some edge in FF, and thus w∈Sw\in S. We have d⁡(w,e2)=d′−d−1d\left(w,e_{2}\right)=d^{\prime}-d-1, where w∈Ld′w\in L_{d^{\prime}}. However, now d⁡(w,v)≥d′−d>d⁡(w,e2)d\left(w,v\right)\geq d^{\prime}-d>d\left(w,e_{2}\right), and ww resolves vv and ee, a contradiction. ∎

As pointed out in [53], if RR is a doubly resolving set that contains a cut-vertex vv, then the set R∖{v}R\setminus\{v\} is also a doubly resolving set. The following observation states that the same result holds for mixed resolving sets, and with certain constraints for (edge) resolving sets.

Observation 11.

Let GG be a connected graph with a cut-vertex vv.

  1. (i)

    Let R⊆V⁡(G)R\subseteq V(G) be such that there are at least two connected components in G−vG-v containing elements of RR. If d⁡(v,x)≠d⁡(v,y)d\left(v,x\right)\neq d\left(v,y\right) for some x,y∈V⁡(G)∪E⁡(G)x,y\in V(G)\cup E(G), then there exists an element s∈Rs\in R, s≠vs\neq v, such that d⁡(s,x)≠d⁡(s,y)d\left(s,x\right)\neq d\left(s,y\right).

  2. (ii)

    If R⊆V⁡(G)R\subseteq V(G) is a mixed resolving set of GG, then every connected component of G−vG-v contains at least one element of RR.

  3. (iii)

    If R⊆V⁡(G)R\subseteq V(G) is a resolving set or edge resolving set of GG, then at most one connected component of G−vG-v does not contain any elements of RR, and that component is isomorphic to PnP_{n} for some n≥1n\geq 1.

Proof.

(i) If s∈Rs\in R is such that the isometric paths from ss to xx and yy go through vv, then we clearly have d⁡(s,x)=d⁡(s,v)+d⁡(v,x)≠d⁡(s,v)+d⁡(v,y)=d⁡(s,y)d\left(s,x\right)=d\left(s,v\right)+d\left(v,x\right)\neq d\left(s,v\right)+d\left(v,y\right)=d\left(s,y\right).

Assume that there are only two connected components G1G_{1}, G2G_{2} of G−vG-v that contain elements of RR, and that x∈V⁡(G1)∪E⁡(G1+v)x\in V(G_{1})\cup E(G_{1}+v) and y∈V⁡(G2)∪E⁡(G2+v)y\in V(G_{2})\cup E(G_{2}+v). Let s1∈V⁡(G1)∩Rs_{1}\in V(G_{1})\cap R and s2∈V⁡(G2)∩Rs_{2}\in V(G_{2})\cap R. Suppose that d⁡(s1,x)=d⁡(s1,y)d\left(s_{1},x\right)=d\left(s_{1},y\right). Now, d⁡(s1,v)+d⁡(v,y)=d⁡(s1,x)≤d⁡(s1,v)+d⁡(v,x)d\left(s_{1},v\right)+d\left(v,y\right)=d\left(s_{1},x\right)\leq d\left(s_{1},v\right)+d\left(v,x\right). Since d⁡(v,x)≠d⁡(v,y)d\left(v,x\right)\neq d\left(v,y\right), we have d⁡(v,y)<d⁡(v,x)d\left(v,y\right)<d\left(v,x\right). Consequently, d⁡(s2,x)=d⁡(s2,v)+d⁡(v,x)>d⁡(s2,v)+d⁡(v,y)≥d⁡(s2,y)d\left(s_{2},x\right)=d\left(s_{2},v\right)+d\left(v,x\right)>d\left(s_{2},v\right)+d\left(v,y\right)\geq d\left(s_{2},y\right). Thus, xx and yy are resolved by s2s_{2}.

(ii) If a connected component G′G^{\prime} does not contain an element of RR, then vv and v​xvx, where x∈V⁡(G′)x\in V(G^{\prime}) are not resolved by RR, a contradiction.

(iii) Easy to see. ∎

The following corollary follows from Propositions 9 and 10, and Observation 11.

Corollary 12.

Let GG be a graph with δ⁡(G)≥2\delta(G)\geq 2.

  1. (i)

    If GG contains a cut-vertex, then edim⁡(G)≤2​c​(G)\mathrm{edim}(G)\leq 2c\left(G\right) and mdim⁡(G)≤2​c​(G)\mathrm{mdim}(G)\leq 2c\left(G\right).

  2. (ii)

    If GG does not contain a cut-vertex, then edim⁡(G)≤2​c​(G)+1\mathrm{edim}(G)\leq 2c\left(G\right)+1 and mdim⁡(G)≤2​c​(G)+1\mathrm{mdim}(G)\leq 2c\left(G\right)+1.

When δ⁡(G)≥2\delta(G)\geq 2, both L⁡(G)=0L(G)=0 and ℓ⁡(G)=0\ell(G)=0. Thus, Corollary 12 proves that when δ⁡(G)≥2\delta(G)\geq 2, Conjecture 1 holds for the edge metric dimension when GG contains a cut-vertex and we are +1 away in the case where GG does not contain a cut-vertex. Compared to Conjecture 2, we are either +1 or +2 away from the conjectured bound for the edge metric dimension depending on whether GG contains a cut-vertex. As for the mixed metric dimension, Corollary 12 proves that Conjecture 3 holds when δ⁡(G)≥2\delta(G)\geq 2 and GG contains a cut-vertex. If δ⁡(G)≥2\delta(G)\geq 2 and the graph does not contain a cut-vertex, we are +1 away from the conjectured bound.

We then turn our attention to graphs with δ⁡(G)=1\delta(G)=1. We will show that a good edge set can be used to construct a (edge, mixed) resolving set also in this case. Moreover, we show that Conjecture 3 holds, and Conjecture 1 holds when L⁡(G)≥1L\left(G\right)\geq 1. We also show that dim(G)\dim(G) and edim⁡(G)\mathrm{edim}(G) are at most 2​c​(G)+12c\left(G\right)+1 when L⁡(G)=0L\left(G\right)=0. We use the following results on trees in our proof.

Proposition 13 ([42]).

Let TT be a tree, and let R⊆V⁡(T)R\subseteq V(T) be the set of leaves of TT. The set RR is a mixed metric basis of TT.

Proposition 14 ([43, 45]).

Let TT be a tree that is not a path. If R⊆V⁡(T)R\subseteq V(T) is a branch-resolving set of TT, then it is a resolving set and an edge resolving set.

Theorem 15.

Let GG be a connected graph that is not a tree such that δ⁡(G)=1\delta(G)=1. Let r∈V⁡(Gb)r\in V(G_{b}), and let S⊆V⁡(Gb)S\subseteq V(G_{b}) contain rr and the endpoints of a good edge set F⊆E⁡(Gb)F\subseteq E(G_{b}) with respect to rr. If RR is a branch-resolving set of GG, then the set R∪SR\cup S is a resolving set and an edge resolving set of GG. If RR is the set of leaves of GG, then the set R∪SR\cup S is a mixed resolving set of GG.

Proof.

Let RR be either a branch-resolving set of GG (for the regular and edge resolving sets) or the set of leaves of GG (for mixed metric dimension). We will show that the set R∪SR\cup S is a (edge, mixed) resolving set of GG.

The graph G−E⁡(Gb)G-E(G_{b}) is a forest (note that some of the trees might be isolated vertices) where each tree contains a unique vertex of GbG_{b}. Let us denote these trees by TvT_{v}, where v∈V⁡(Gb)∩V⁡(Tv)v\in V(G_{b})\cap V(T_{v}).

Consider distinct x,y∈V⁡(G)∪E⁡(G)x,y\in V(G)\cup E(G). We will show that xx and yy are resolved by R∪SR\cup S.

  • •

    Assume that x,y∈V⁡(Tv)∪E⁡(Tv)x,y\in V(T_{v})\cup E(T_{v}) for some v∈V⁡(Gb)v\in V(G_{b}). Denote Rv=(V⁡(Tv)∩R)∪{v}R_{v}=(V(T_{v})\cap R)\cup\{v\}. The set RvR_{v} is a (edge, mixed) resolving set of TvT_{v} by Propositions 14 and 13. If xx and yy are resolved by some element in RvR_{v} that is not vv, then we are done. If xx and yy are resolved by vv, then they are resolved by any element in S∖{v}S\setminus\{v\}. Since GG is not a tree, the set S∖{v}S\setminus\{v\} is clearly nonempty, and xx and yy are resolved in GG.

  • •

    Assume that x,y∈V⁡(Gb)∪E⁡(Gb)x,y\in V(G_{b})\cup E(G_{b}). Now xx and yy are resolved by SS due to Theorem 8, Proposition 9 or Proposition 10.

  • •

    Assume that x∈V⁡(Tv)∪E⁡(Tv)x\in V(T_{v})\cup E(T_{v}) and y∈V⁡(Tw)∪E⁡(Tw)y\in V(T_{w})\cup E(T_{w}) where v,w∈V⁡(Gb)v,w\in V(G_{b}), v≠wv\neq w. The set SS is a doubly resolving set of GbG_{b} according to Theorem 8. Thus, there exist distinct s,t∈Ss,t\in S such that d⁡(s,v)−d⁡(s,w)≠d⁡(t,v)−d⁡(t,w)d\left(s,v\right)-d\left(s,w\right)\neq d\left(t,v\right)-d\left(t,w\right). Suppose to the contrary that d⁡(s,x)=d⁡(s,y)d\left(s,x\right)=d\left(s,y\right) and d⁡(t,x)=d⁡(t,y)d\left(t,x\right)=d\left(t,y\right). Now we have

    d⁡(w,y)−d⁡(v,x)=d⁡(s,v)−d⁡(s,w)≠d⁡(t,v)−d⁡(t,w)=d⁡(w,y)−d⁡(v,x),d\left(w,y\right)-d\left(v,x\right)=d\left(s,v\right)-d\left(s,w\right)\neq d\left(t,v\right)-d\left(t,w\right)=d\left(w,y\right)-d\left(v,x\right),

    a contradiction. Thus, ss or tt resolves xx and yy.

  • •

    Assume that x∈V⁡(Tv)∪E⁡(Tv)x\in V(T_{v})\cup E(T_{v}) for some v∈V⁡(Gb)v\in V(G_{b}), v≠xv\neq x, and y=y1​y2∈E⁡(Gb)y=y_{1}y_{2}\in E(G_{b}). Suppose that d⁡(r,x)=d⁡(r,y)d\left(r,x\right)=d\left(r,y\right). Without loss of generality, we may assume that d⁡(r,y)=d⁡(r,y1)=dd\left(r,y\right)=d\left(r,y_{1}\right)=d. Now y1∈Ldy_{1}\in L_{d} and v∈Ld−dxv\in L_{d-d_{x}}, where dx=d⁡(v,x)∈{0,…,d}d_{x}=d\left(v,x\right)\in\{0,\ldots,d\}. If y2∈Ldy_{2}\in L_{d}, then yy is a horizontal edge and y1,y2∈Sy_{1},y_{2}\in S. Now xx and yy are resolved by y1y_{1} or y2y_{2}. So assume that y2∈Ld+1y_{2}\in L_{d+1}. Let z∈V⁡(Gb)z\in V(G_{b}) be a leaf in TFT_{F} such that y2y_{2} lies on a path from rr to zz in TFT_{F}. Since δ⁡(Gb)≥2\delta(G_{b})\geq 2, the vertex zz is an endpoint of some edge in FF, and thus z∈Sz\in S. Now z∈Ld′z\in L_{d^{\prime}} for some d′>d+1d^{\prime}>d+1 and d⁡(z,y2)=d′−d−1d\left(z,y_{2}\right)=d^{\prime}-d-1 by Lemma 6. Consequently,

    d⁡(z,x)=d⁡(z,v)+dx≥d′−(d−dx)+dx=2​dx+1+d⁡(z,y2)>d⁡(z,y).d\left(z,x\right)=d\left(z,v\right)+d_{x}\geq d^{\prime}-(d-d_{x})+d_{x}=2d_{x}+1+d\left(z,y_{2}\right)>d\left(z,y\right).

∎

Since the root rr can be chosen freely, we can choose the root to be a cut-vertex in GG whenever GG contains cut-vertices. The bounds in the next corollary then follow from Observations 7 and 11, and Theorem 15.

Corollary 16.

Let GG be a connected graph that is not a tree such that δ⁡(G)=1\delta(G)=1. We have dim(G)≤λ⁡(G)+2​c​(G)\dim(G)\leq\lambda(G)+2c\left(G\right), edim⁡(G)≤λ⁡(G)+2​c​(G)\mathrm{edim}(G)\leq\lambda(G)+2c\left(G\right), and mdim⁡(G)≤ℓ⁡(G)+2​c​(G)\mathrm{mdim}(G)\leq\ell\left(G\right)+2c\left(G\right),

dim(G)≤λ⁡(G)+2​c​(G),edim⁡(G)≤λ⁡(G)+2​c​(G),mdim⁡(G)≤ℓ⁡(G)+2​c​(G),\dim(G)\leq\lambda(G)+2c\left(G\right),\qquad\mathrm{edim}(G)\leq\lambda(G)+2c\left(G\right),\qquad\mathrm{mdim}(G)\leq\ell\left(G\right)+2c\left(G\right),

where λ⁡(G)=max⁡{L⁡(G),1}\lambda(G)=\max\{L\left(G\right),1\}.

The relationship of metric dimension and edge metric dimension has garnered a lot of attention since the edge metric dimension was introduced. Zubrilina [76] showed that the ratio edim⁡(G)dim(G)\frac{\mathrm{edim}(G)}{\dim(G)} cannot be bounded from above by a constant, and Knor et al. [46] showed the same for the ratio dim(G)edim⁡(G)\frac{\dim(G)}{\mathrm{edim}(G)}. Inspired by this, Sedlar and Škrekovski [62] conjectured that for a graph G≠K2G\neq K_{2}, we have |dim(G)−edim⁡(G)|≤c⁡(G)|\dim(G)-\mathrm{edim}(G)|\leq c\left(G\right). This bound, if true, is tight due to the construction presented in [46]. It is easy to see that dim(G)≥λ⁡(G)\dim(G)\geq\lambda(G) and edim⁡(G)≥λ⁡(G)\mathrm{edim}(G)\geq\lambda(G) (the fact that dim(G)≥L⁡(G)\dim(G)\geq L\left(G\right) is shown explicitly in [15], for example). Thus, we now obtain the bound |dim(G)−edim⁡(G)|≤2​c​(G)|\dim(G)-\mathrm{edim}(G)|\leq 2c\left(G\right) due to the bounds established in Corollaries 12 and 16.

4 Geodetic sets and variants

We now address the problems related to geodetic sets, and show that the same method can be applied in this context as well. Note that all leaves of a graph belong to any of its geodetic sets.

We first study geodetic sets explicitly, as this is the most well-studied notion in this area. We then address monitoring edge-geodetic sets and distance edge-monitoring sets, because these two notions have been studied in the literature in relation to the cyclomatic number and the number of leaves. Bounds for other related parameters in Figure 1 follow from the result on monitoring edge-geodetic sets.

4.1 Geodetic sets

Let g⁡(G)g\left(G\right) denote the size of a smallest geodetic set of a graph GG.

Theorem 17.

Let GG be a connected graph. If GG has a cut-vertex then g⁡(G)≤2​c​(G)+ℓ⁡(G)g\left(G\right)\leq 2c\left(G\right)+\ell\left(G\right). Otherwise, g⁡(G)≤2​c​(G)+1g\left(G\right)\leq 2c\left(G\right)+1.

Proof.

Let FF be a set of good edges of GG with respect to a vertex rr obtained by Lemma 5. When GG has a cut-vertex then rr shall be a cut-vertex. Let SS be the union of the set of leaf vertices of GG and the endpoints of the edges in FF. If GG is biconnected then include rr in SS also. Clearly, |S|≤2​c​(G)+1+ℓ⁡(G)|S|\leq 2c\left(G\right)+1+\ell\left(G\right) when GG is biconnected and |S|≤2​c​(G)+ℓ⁡(G)|S|\leq 2c\left(G\right)+\ell\left(G\right), otherwise. Due to Lemma 6, TFT_{F} is a tree and let LL be the set of leaf vertices of TFT_{F}.

If GG is biconnected, due to Lemma 6, L∪{r}L\cup\{r\} is a geodetic set of GG, and clearly (L∪{r})⊆S(L\cup\{r\})\subseteq S. Therefore SS is a geodetic set of GG.

Otherwise, rr is a cut-vertex and L⊆SL\subseteq S. Consider any vertex uu of GG. Let CuC_{u} denote the connected component of G−{r}G-\{r\} containing uu. Due to Lemma 6, uu lies in an isometric path between rr and a vertex u′∈V⁡(Cu)∩Lu^{\prime}\in V(C_{u})\cap L. Since rr is a cut-vertex there exists a connected component C′C^{\prime} different from CuC_{u} and L∩V⁡(C′)L\cap V(C^{\prime}) is non-empty. Let u′′u^{\prime\prime} be a vertex of L∩V⁡(C′)L\cap V(C^{\prime}). Clearly d⁡(u′,u′′)=d⁡(r,u′)+d⁡(r,u′′)d\left(u^{\prime},u^{\prime\prime}\right)=d\left(r,u^{\prime}\right)+d\left(r,u^{\prime\prime}\right). Let P′P^{\prime} be the path in TFT_{F} between rr and u′u^{\prime} and P′′P^{\prime\prime} be the path in TFT_{F} between rr and u′′u^{\prime\prime}. We have that P=P′∪P′′P=P^{\prime}\cup P^{\prime\prime} is an isometric path in GG and contains uu. Hence, the set LL is a geodetic set of GG, SS is a geodetic set of GG. ∎

The upper bound of Theorem 17 is tight when there is a cut-vertex, indeed, consider the graph formed by a disjoint union of kk odd cycles and ll paths, all identified via a single vertex. The obtained graph has cyclomatic number kk, ll leaves, and geodetic number 2​k+l2k+l. Observe that any odd cycle has geodetic number 3 and cyclomatic number 1, so the bound g⁡(G)≤2​c​(G)+1g\left(G\right)\leq 2c\left(G\right)+1 is tight when there is no cut-vertex in the graph. However, we do not know the best possible bound for 2-connected graphs with arbitrarily large values of c⁡(G)c(G). The graph GkG_{k} obtained from K2,kK_{2,k} by adding an edge between the two vertices of degree kk is 2-connected, has cyclomatic number kk and geodetic number kk. We do not know a family of 2-connected graphs of arbitrarily large cyclomatic number whose geodetic number is closer to twice the cyclomatic number and leave this as an open problem.

4.2 Monitoring edge-geodetic sets

Let meg⁡(G)\mathrm{meg}\left(G\right) denote the size of a smallest monitoring edge-geodetic set of a graph GG. It was proved in [33] that meg⁡(G)≤9​c​(G)+ℓ⁡(G)−8\mathrm{meg}\left(G\right)\leq 9c\left(G\right)+\ell\left(G\right)-8 for every graph GG, and some graphs were constructed for which meg⁡(G)=3​c​(G)+ℓ⁡(G)\mathrm{meg}\left(G\right)=3c\left(G\right)+\ell\left(G\right). We next improve the former upper bound, therefore showing that the latter construction is essentially best possible.

Theorem 18.

For any graph GG, we have meg⁡(G)≤3​c​(G)+ℓ⁡(G)+1\mathrm{meg}\left(G\right)\leq 3c\left(G\right)+\ell\left(G\right)+1. If GG contains a cut-vertex, then meg⁡(G)≤3​c​(G)+ℓ⁡(G)\mathrm{meg}\left(G\right)\leq 3c\left(G\right)+\ell\left(G\right).

Proof.

It is not hard to check that when GG is a tree, we have meg⁡(G)=ℓ⁡(G)\mathrm{meg}\left(G\right)=\ell\left(G\right) [33]. Let us thus assume that c⁡(G)≥1c\left(G\right)\geq 1.

We will first show the bound meg⁡(G)≤3​c​(G)+ℓ⁡(G)+1\mathrm{meg}\left(G\right)\leq 3c\left(G\right)+\ell\left(G\right)+1. We say that an edge ee is monitored by a set SS if there are two vertices x,yx,y of SS such that ee lies on all isometric paths between xx and yy; SS is thus a monitoring edge-geodetic set of GG if it monitors all edges of GG.

Let rr be an arbitrary vertex of GG that belongs to some cycle of GG, and let FF be a good set of edges (with respect to rr) obtained through Lemma 5. We construct a set SS as follows: rr belongs to SS, all leaves of GG belong to SS, and for each edge of FF, both its endpoints belong to SS. Moreover, for each vertex uu of GG with |Br​(u)|≥2|B_{r}(u)|\geq 2, we add to SS all endpoints of the edges of Br​(u)B_{r}(u) (not just the |Br​(u)|−1|B_{r}(u)|-1 ones that are in FF).

It is clear that we have |S|≤3​|F|+ℓ⁡(G)+1|S|\leq 3|F|+\ell\left(G\right)+1, since we add to SS at most two vertices for each edge in FF, with an additional vertex whenever there is a vertical edge in FF (this can only happen |F||F| times). By Observation 7, we have |F|≤c⁡(G)|F|\leq c\left(G\right), and so |S|≤3​c​(G)+ℓ⁡(G)+1|S|\leq 3c\left(G\right)+\ell\left(G\right)+1.

We now show that SS is a monitoring edge-geodetic set. Let e=u​ve=uv be an edge of GG. If both endpoints u,vu,v of ee are in SS, then ee is clearly monitored by them. In particular, this is the case if ee is horizontal with respect to rr.

Assume that ee has at most one endpoint in SS. Thus ee is vertical with respect to rr, and ee is also an edge in TFT_{F}. Let us consider the tree TFT_{F} further, and remove the additional edges of the sets Br​(w)B_{r}(w) whose endpoints we added to SS, i.e. all edges in some Br​(w)B_{r}(w) where |Br​(w)|≥2|B_{r}(w)|\geq 2. The resulting graph is a forest where each tree can be rooted in a natural way by following the structure of TFT_{F} when the root is rr. Of these trees, every root and every leaf is in SS. Moreover, the edge ee is an edge in one such tree. Consider a leaf ll and a root r′r^{\prime} of one tree TT. Now there is in fact a unique isometric path between ll and r′r^{\prime} in GG, and this path is completely contained in TT (otherwise, there is a vertical edge whose endpoints we added to SS in the path between ll and r′r^{\prime} in TT, and ll is not in the same tree as r′r^{\prime}, a contradiction). Thus, ee is monitored by a leaf and the root of the tree that contains ee.

Assume then that GG contains a cut-vertex. Since the root rr can be arbitrarily, we can choose rr to be a cut-vertex. Now the set S∖{r}S\setminus\{r\} is a monitoring edge-geodetic set. Indeed, if rr and u∈Su\in S monitor an edge ee, then ee is also monitored by uu and v∈Sv\in S where vv is in a different connected component of G−rG-r as uu. Thus, when GG contains a cut-vertex, we have meg⁡(G)≤3​c​(G)+ℓ⁡(G)\mathrm{meg}\left(G\right)\leq 3c\left(G\right)+\ell\left(G\right). ∎

4.3 Distance-edge-monitoring-sets

We now turn our attention to distance-edge-monitoring-sets and prove Conjecture 4. Let dem⁡(G)\mathrm{dem}\left(G\right) denote the size of a smallest distance-edge-monitoring set of a graph GG. We shall use the following lemma.

Lemma 19 ([30, Observation 4]).

For any graph GG, any distance-edge-monitoring-set of its base graph GbG_{b} is also one of GG.

Theorem 20.

For any connected graph GG, dem⁡(G)≤c⁡(G)+1\mathrm{dem}\left(G\right)\leq c\left(G\right)+1.

Proof.

We say that an edge ee is monitored by a set SS if there are two vertices x∈Sx\in S and y∈V⁡(G)y\in V(G) such that ee lies on all isometric paths between xx and yy; SS is thus a monitoring edge-geodetic set of GG if it monitors all edges of GG.

The statement is true when c⁡(G)≤2c\left(G\right)\leq 2 by [30], so we can assume GG is not a tree. By Lemma 19, we may assume GG has minimum degree at least 2.

Let rr be an arbitrary vertex of GG, and let FF be a good set of edges (with respect to rr) obtained through Lemma 5. We construct a set SS as follows: rr belongs to SS, and for each edge of FF, one of its endpoints belongs to SS; if the edge is vertical with respect to rr, we choose the endpoint that is farthest from rr; if it is horizontal, we choose any of the two endpoints.

It is clear that |S|≤c⁡(G)+1|S|\leq c\left(G\right)+1, as |S|≤|F|+1|S|\leq|F|+1 and |F|≤c⁡(G)|F|\leq c\left(G\right) by Observation 7. We next show that SS is distance-edge-monitoring.

Let e=u​ve=uv be an edge of GG. If ee is an edge of FF, it is monitored by SS, since one of its endpoints is in SS. Thus, we can assume that ee is not in FF. Hence, it is vertical with respect to rr, and we assume without loss of generality that d⁡(u,r)=d⁡(v,r)+1d\left(u,r\right)=d\left(v,r\right)+1. Since ee is not in FF, we have |Br​(u)|=1|B_{r}(u)|=1. Thus, all isometric paths from uu to rr go through ee, and hence ee is monitored by SS. Thus all edges are monitored by SS, which establishes the claim. ∎

5 Path covers/partitions and variants

In this section, we consider the path covering and partition problems. We focus on isometric path edge-covers (sets of isometric paths that cover all edges of the graph) and on isometric path partitions (sets of isometric paths that partition the vertex set of the graph). Indeed, those have the most restrictive definitions and the obtained bounds thus hold for the other related path covering/partition problems from Figure 1. We denote by isopec⁡(G)\mathrm{isopec}\left(G\right) and by isopp⁡(G)\mathrm{isopp}\left(G\right), respectively, the smallest size of an isometric path edge-cover and isometric path (vertex-)partition, respectively.

5.1 Isometric path edge-cover

Theorem 21.

For any graph GG, isopec⁡(G)≤3​c​(G)+⌈(ℓ⁡(G)+1)/2⌉\mathrm{isopec}\left(G\right)\leq 3c\left(G\right)+\lceil(\ell\left(G\right)+1)/2\rceil.

Proof.

We construct a set SS of paths as follows. Consider the base graph GbG_{b} of GG, let rr be an arbitrary vertex of GbG_{b}, and let FF be a good set of edges of GbG_{b} (with respect to rr) obtained by Lemma 5. For each horizontal edge x​yxy of FF, we add it (as a path) to SS, as well as an isometric path from xx to rr and one from yy to rr. For each vertex vv with |Br​(v)|≥2|B_{r}(v)|\geq 2, we add to SS, |Br​(v)||B_{r}(v)| isometric paths from vv to rr, each starting with a different edge from Br​(v)B_{r}(v). Finally, if GG contains some leaves, we consider the set L′L^{\prime} formed by the set LL of leaves of GG, together with the vertex rr, and an arbitrary pairing of L′L^{\prime}, of size ⌈(ℓ⁡(G)+1)/2⌉\lceil(\ell\left(G\right)+1)/2\rceil, such that each vertex of L′L^{\prime} is paired with some other one (if ℓ⁡(G)+1\ell\left(G\right)+1 is odd, one vertex of L′L^{\prime} may be paired with two vertices, but all others are paired with one only).

Consider a set S′S^{\prime} of ⌈(ℓ⁡(G)+1)/2⌉\lceil(\ell\left(G\right)+1)/2\rceil isometric paths between each two mutually paired vertices of L′L^{\prime}. We incrementally modify the pairing as follows. If all edges of G−E⁡(Gb)G-E(G_{b}) are covered by S′S^{\prime}, we do nothing. Otherwise, assume some edge ee of G−E⁡(Gb)G-E(G_{b}) is not covered by a path of S′S^{\prime}. Note that G−E⁡(Gb)G-E(G_{b}) is a forest, and ee is a bridge of GG, with one component of G−eG-e containing at least one leaf, and one component containing rr. Since that leaf and rr are paired vertices in L′L^{\prime} but ee is not covered by the isometric paths in S′S^{\prime}, there must exist two pairs {a,b}\{a,b\} and {c,d}\{c,d\} of paired vertices of L′L^{\prime}, each pair being in one component of G−eG-e, say aa and bb are in a tree component of G−eG-e and c,dc,d are in the same component as rr. We modify the pairing of L′L^{\prime} by replacing {a,b}\{a,b\} and {c,d}\{c,d\} by {a,c}\{a,c\} and {b,d}\{b,d\}, and we claim that the isometric paths induced by this new pairing cover the same edges from G−E⁡(Gb)G-E(G_{b}) as before, and also, the edge ee. Indeed, as G−E⁡(Gb)G-E(G_{b}) is a forest (and each component of G−E⁡(Gb)G-E(G_{b}) has a unique vertex with neighbors in GbG_{b}), any isometric path (in GG) from a leaf to any vertex of the same component of G−E⁡(Gb)G-E(G_{b}) is unique. Thus, the a−ba-b isometric path is unique, and any isometric path from aa to cc (and from bb to dd) goes through ee. Hence, the union of any two such isometric paths contains the edges of the a−ba-b path. A similar argument holds for the path from cc to dd. Thus, we continue this process until all edges of G−E⁡(Gb)G-E(G_{b}) are covered by S′S^{\prime}, increasing the number of covered edges at each step. Finally, we add S′S^{\prime} to SS.

It is clear that SS contains only isometric paths, by construction; moreover, |S|≤3​c​(G)+⌈(ℓ⁡(G)+1)/2⌉|S|\leq 3c\left(G\right)+\lceil(\ell\left(G\right)+1)/2\rceil because we add at most three paths to SS for each edge of FF in the first steps of the construction, and the last step of the construction adds ⌈(ℓ⁡(G)+1)/2⌉\lceil(\ell\left(G\right)+1)/2\rceil additional paths to SS. It remains to show that SS covers all edges of GG. Let ee be an edge. If ee is an edge of G−E⁡(Gb)G-E(G_{b}), by the last part of the construction of SS, ee is covered by some isometric path between two vertices of L′L^{\prime}. If ee is a horizontal edge with respect to rr, then ee itself is a path of SS, so ee is covered. If ee is a vertical edge with respect to rr and ee belongs to GbG_{b}, then there must be a vertex ww of GbG_{b} with |Br​(w)|≥2|B_{r}(w)|\geq 2 and ee lies on an isometric path from ww to rr. Let ww be chosen so as to be the closest to ee, among all such vertices. Then, we have selected some isometric path from ww to rr in the first step of the construction, each containing a distinct edge of Br​(w)B_{r}(w). By the choice of ww, one such path from ww to rr goes through ee, and thus ee is covered. ∎

The upper bound of Theorem 21 is nearly tight, indeed, consider (again) the graph formed by a disjoint union of kk odd cycles and ll paths, all identified via a single vertex. The obtained graph has cyclomatic number kk, ll leaves, and isometric path edge-cover number 3​k+⌈l/2⌉3k+\lceil l/2\rceil.

5.2 Isometric path partition

Theorem 22.

For any graph GG, isopp⁡(G)≤2​c​(G)+ℓ⁡(G)\mathrm{isopp}\left(G\right)\leq 2c\left(G\right)+\ell\left(G\right).

Proof.

The proof is similar to the one of Theorem 21, except that it is not necessary to consider the base graph. Consider an arbitrary vertex rr of GG, and let FF be a good set of edges of GG (with respect to rr) obtained by Lemma 5. We construct a set SS of isometric vertex-disjoint paths as follows. Initially, S=∅S=\emptyset. For each horizontal edge x​yxy of FF, we consider an isometric path PxP_{x} from xx to rr and an isometric path PyP_{y} from yy to rr. We first add to SS the maximal subpath of PxP_{x} (starting at rr), that does not overlap with any path already in SS. Then, we do the same for PyP_{y}. Similarly, for each vertex vv with |Br​(v)|≥2|B_{r}(v)|\geq 2, we let NvN_{v} be the set of vertices uu with u​v∈Br​(v)uv\in B_{r}(v). We consider an arbitrary isometric path from vv to rr (it goes through some vertex, say u0u_{0}, of NvN_{v}). Then, for every vertex u∈Nv∖{u0}u\in N_{v}\setminus\{u_{0}\}, we sequentially consider an isometric path PuP_{u} from uu to rr. We proceed as before for each of these paths: we add to SS a maximal subpath of PxP_{x} starting at xx, that does not intersect any path already in SS. Finally, for every leaf vv of GG, we again consider an isometric path from vv to rr, and select its maximal subpath (starting from vv) that does not intersect any other path in PP.

We have added at most 2​c​(G)+ℓ⁡(G)2c\left(G\right)+\ell(G) paths to SS (at most two for every edge in FF and at most one for every leaf). By construction, SS contains only isometric paths, and they are pairwise vertex-disjoint. By similar arguments as in the proof of Theorem 21, every vertex is covered by a path of SS, and so we have obtained an isometric path partition of the desired size. ∎

Once again, the bound is nearly tight by the same graph formed by a disjoint union of kk odd cycles (each of length at least 5) and ll paths, all identified via a single vertex. It has cyclomatic number kk, ll leaves, and isometric path partition number 2​k+l−12k+l-1.

We remark that for many graphs, the bound of ℓ⁡(G)\ell(G) to cover the leaves of the graph in the above theorem is not necessarily tight. Indeed, for some trees, one may have an (isometric) path partition of size ⌈ℓ⁡(G)/2⌉\lceil\ell\left(G\right)/2\rceil: consider for example a path PtP_{t} on t≥3t\geq 3 vertices and for each of its t−2t-2 internal vertices, say vv, attach a copy of P3P_{3} whose central vertex is made adjacent to vv. This tree has 2​t−22t-2 leaves and a path partition of size t−1t-1.

In fact, it is known that one gets a more precise (always tight) bound for the path partition number of a tree by considering its scattering number, see [39].

6 Algorithmic consequences

As mentioned in the introduction, for many of the problems studied here, there are no efficient algorithms for graphs of bounded treewidth: for example, it is NP-hard to compute the metric dimension or the geodetic number of graphs of constant treewidth (in fact, even pathwidth) [50, 68]. The complexity of the strong geodetic set problem with respect to treewidth is unknown [21].

Recall that the treewidth is at most the cyclomatic number plus one. Next, we show that for the vertex-subset problems studied in this paper, our bounds imply polynomial-time (XP) algorithms for graphs of bounded cyclomatic number, thus partially answering some algorithmic open problems in this area.

Theorem 23.

For all the variants of geodetic sets and metric dimension considered in this paper, if we have an upper bound on the solution size of a⋅c⁡(G)+f⁡(ℓ⁡(G))a\cdot c\left(G\right)+f(\ell\left(G\right)) for some a∈ℕa\in\mathbb{N}, we obtain an algorithm with running time O⁡(na⋅c⁡(G))O(n^{a\cdot c\left(G\right)}) on graphs GG of order nn.

Proof.

The algorithm needs to pre-process the leaves and compute a subset of the leaves of size f⁡(ℓ⁡(G))f(\ell\left(G\right)). This can be done in polynomial time for all the considered problems. For geodetic set types of problems, one simply selects all the leaves (for distance-edge-monitoring sets, we must not select any leaf). This can be done in time O⁡(n+c⁡(G))=O⁡(n2)O(n+c\left(G\right))=O(n^{2}). For metric dimension related problems, one has to compute the structural shape of the leaves; this can be done in time O⁡(n+c⁡(G))O(n+c\left(G\right)) as well, see for example [24, 45].

After that (and noting that selecting f⁡(ℓ⁡(G))f(\ell\left(G\right)) leaves of GG is necessary in each of the considered problems), the proofs of our bounds show that a⋅c⁡(G)a\cdot c\left(G\right) are sufficient to extend the chosen leaf subset to a solution. It thus suffices to iterate over all possible subsets of vertices of size at most a⋅c⁡(G)a\cdot c\left(G\right): consider this as a potential solution, and add the required set of leaves to the solution, and check whether it is a valid solution. This yields the desired running time. ∎

7 Conclusion

We have demonstrated that a simple technique based on breadth-first-search is very efficient to obtain bounds for many distance-based covering problems, when the cyclomatic number and the number of leaves are considered. This resolves or advances several open problems and conjectures from the literature on this type of problems. There remain some gaps between the obtained bounds and the conjectures or known constructions, that still need to be closed. Moreover, in some cases, obtaining the best possible upper bound for 2-connected graphs of arbitrarily large cyclomatic number is also an interesting open problem, for example for the geodetic number and the monitoring-edge geodetic number.

A refinement of the cyclomatic number of a (connected) graph GG is called its max leaf number, which is the maximum number of leaves in a spanning tree of GG. It is known that the cyclomatic number is always upper-bounded by a quadratic function of the max leaf number plus the number of leaves [22], so, all our bounds also imply bounds using the max leaf number only.

Regarding the algorithmic applications, we note that the XP algorithms described in Theorem 23 can sometimes be improved to obtain an FPT algorithm. This is the case for geodetic sets [44], but whether this is possible for the metric dimension remains a major open problem [22, 44] (this is however shown to be possible for the larger parameter “max leaf number” [22]).

Also, we leave open whether similar algorithms can be obtained for the path covering/partition problems studied here. As one has to decide where the paths go through, it seems a little bit more difficult to design such an algorithm than for the vertex-subset problems. This would be quite interesting, as the complexity of the isometric path cover problem with respect to treewidth is unknown [21].

We have not been exhaustive. There might be other distance-based covering problems for which the same approach can be used. For example, this is the case for the problem of geodesic-transversal [56] (also called maximal shortest path cover in [61]): a set SS of vertices of a graph GG such that every maximal isometric path of GG contains a vertex of SS.

Another distance-related problem which has been studied in relation with the cyclomatic number is the edge-tracking path problem [16], a variant of the more studied (vertex)-tracking path problem [5, 16, 23]. It is shown in [16] that the edge-tracking path problem can be reduced to essentially finding a feedback edge set of the graph. This result also implies that the size of an optimal (vertex)-tracking path set is at most twice the cyclomatic number. Note that, however, the tracking path problem is known to be efficiently solvable for graphs of bounded treewidth [23], hence it behaves differently from most problems studied here.

For other distance-based parameters, the type of bounds that are studied here do not hold. For example, this is the case for strong metric dimension, that is more constrained than the metric dimension: a solution requires half of the vertices for any cycle graph [59] (which has cyclomatic number 1).

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research.
